analysis.one_liner: Requires all new cars to come equipped with automatic emergency braking and other crash-avoidance technology.
analysis.headline: The bill to mandate crash-avoidance technology in all new cars died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to write safety rules requiring every new passenger car sold in the United States to include five crash-avoidance technologies: automatic emergency braking (forward and reverse), rear cross-traffic warning, lane departure warning, and blind spot warning. It would also have required better headlights and research into driver-monitoring systems, with consumer information about what driver-assistance features can and cannot do. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, passengers, pedestrians, bicyclists, and other people on the road, who would face fewer crashes and less severe ones. The bill's text specifically names protection for pedestrians, bicyclists, and other vulnerable road users [S3]. Federal safety research has found that automatic emergency braking substantially reduces rear-end crashes, so a mandate would prevent injuries and deaths and save families the cost of crashes.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every new passenger car sold in the U.S. to be equipped with forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking that detects vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists and applies the brakes automatically [S3].

Requires rear automatic emergency braking, rear cross-traffic warning, lane departure warning, and blind spot warning on all new passenger vehicles, with rules that ensure the systems work at real-world city and highway speeds [S3].
Requires upgraded headlight rules to improve road illumination, prevent glare, and set performance standards for automatic high beams and curve-adaptive headlamps [S3].

Directs DOT to research driver-monitoring systems that prevent over-reliance on automation, and to require clear point-of-sale information about what driver-assistance systems can and cannot do, so buyers are not misled by marketing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would have to install the required sensors and software as standard equipment within two model years of the final rules, with some of that cost likely passed on to new-car buyers. New-car prices could rise modestly, though the technology is already common in many models and becomes cheaper as production scales.

drawbacks.text: Mandating five technologies as standard equipment would raise the cost of every new vehicle, a real burden for lower-income buyers in a market where new cars are already expensive; the bill includes no mechanism to offset those costs [S3].

The bill sets fixed deadlines (final rules within two years, compliance within two model years) without funding for the Department of Transportation to conduct the rulemaking, testing, and research it demands, which raises the risk of rushed or delayed standards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Crash-avoidance technology is one of the most cost-effective safety measures available: the systems address human error, the leading cause of crashes, and much of the hardware is already offered on many models, so the mandate's main effect is to make it universal rather than optional. The main honest objection is the added cost to entry-level buyers, which could be modest if the equipment is already partially on the vehicle. On balance the safety gains for everyone on the road outweigh the price increase, though the bill's aggressive deadlines without funding are a design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 13, 2020, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, since bills that are not passed expire with the Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because the bill died: they avoid a federal requirement to make crash-avoidance technology standard equipment on every new vehicle, keeping it as an optional, price-able feature instead. People killed or injured in preventable crashes bear the cost of the delay.

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, where it received no further action

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over vehicle safety standards
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but never scheduled a hearing or markup, keeping the bill from advancing

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no votes ever held, the record shows no measurable support or opposition from either party beyond the sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to make crash-avoidance systems standard equipment on every new vehicle within two model years, converting features they currently sell as optional upgrades into mandatory costs. It died in committee, so that cost never materialized.

industries.industry: Automotive safety technology and sensor suppliers
industries.note: A universal mandate would have guaranteed a market for radar, camera, and braking-system suppliers. With the bill dead, growth in this market continues to depend on voluntary adoption and regulatory pressure rather than a requirement.
